questions.q: Activities of daily living per the page split into which two groups?
opts: Basic (self-care related) and instrumental (handling own phone, money, etc.)
questions.exp: ADL: basic = self-care related; instrumental = handling own phone, money, etc. Cognitive impairment: minor = ADL unaffected; major = ADL affected. (Book p572)

questions.q: The book's dementia definition: major cognitive impairment plus how many of the 6 cognitive domains affected?
questions.exp: Definition as printed: major cognitive impairment + >=1 out of 6 cognitive domains affected. (Book p572)

questions.q: The language domain in the 6-domain table maps to which areas?
opts: Inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's) and superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's)
questions.exp: Domain table: episodic memory -> hippocampus (median temporal lobe); language -> inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's) + superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's); complex attention, executive function and social cognition -> prefrontal cortex; perceptual motor (praxicons) -> superior parietal lobule. (Book p572)

questions.q: The four causes of dementia listed on this page are:
opts: Alzheimer's disease (m/c), diffuse Lewy body dementia, vascular dementia, normal pressure hydrocephalus
questions.exp: Causes: 1. Alzheimer's disease (m/c); 2. diffuse Lewy body (DLB) dementia; 3. vascular dementia (branches: post-stroke, multi-infarct dementia, white matter dementia/Binswanger disease); 4. normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). (Book p572)

questions.q: Based on the parts of brain affected, the subcortical-dementia list includes:
opts: DLB dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy, Binswanger disease, NPH
questions.exp: Dementia -> cortical; subcortical -> diffuse Lewy body (DLB) dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy, Binswanger disease, NPH. (Book p572)

questions.q: The PFC-functions note assigns which function to the orbital PFC?
questions.exp: Note - functions of PFC: dorsolateral PFC executive function; medial PFC energisation and motivation; orbital PFC behaviour. (Book p572)

questions.q: A reversible-cause workup lists benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants and lithium under which mnemonic letter?
questions.exp: Reversible causes: D drugs (benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants, lithium); E endocrine (hypothyroidism: metabolic slowing); M metabolic (vit B12 deficiency); E chronic infections of ear; N normal pressure hydrocephalus; T trauma, tumors; I infections (chronic meningitis); A anemia, autoimmune encephalitis. (Book p573)

questions.q: Peripheral neuropathy plus dementia plus subacute combined cord degeneration points to which reversible cause?
questions.exp: Note: vit B12 deficiency -> peripheral neuropathy, dementia and subacute combined cord degeneration; Rx of NPH: surgery. (Book p573)

questions.q: The treatment of NPH stated in the reversible-causes note is:
questions.exp: Note under reversible causes: Rx of NPH - surgery. (Book p573)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the condition NOT listed under young-onset dementia:
questions.exp: Young onset dementia: frontotemporal dementia (Pick's disease) m/c, prion disease, Huntington's disease, DLB dementia. (Book p573)

questions.q: Among rapidly progressive dementias, which two are bracketed as non-degenerative?
questions.exp: Rapidly progressive: FTD (Pick's) m/c, prion, DLB, HIV and Whipple's (bracketed non-degenerative), tumors (based on location). (Book p573)

questions.q: The pathology note says entorhinal cortex atrophy is specific for which disease?
questions.exp: Atrophy of: entorhinal cortex - specific for Alzheimer's; dentate nucleus - occurs with ageing. Alzheimer's disease: m/c cause of dementia; most important risk factor age; sporadic. (Book p573)

questions.q: The book prints what chance of Alzheimer's for age >85 years?
questions.exp: Most important risk factor: age (>85 years: 40% chance of Alzheimer's). (Book p573)

questions.q: In the APP pathway, abnormal kinetics with metabolism by which enzyme produces A-beta amyloid (beta-pleated sheets)?
questions.exp: APP (amyloid precursor protein, gene on chr 21) with abnormal kinetics is metabolised by beta-secretase producing A-beta amyloid (beta-pleated sheets); note: normal metabolism uses alpha-secretase. (Book p574)

questions.q: A-beta 40 and A-beta 42 diverge in the pathway: which outcome pairs with A-beta 40?
opts: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy with microhemorrhages in brain
questions.exp: A-beta 40 -> cerebral amyloid angiopathy (microhemorrhages in brain); A-beta 42 -> Alzheimer's disease -> depositions of hyperphosphorylated tau proteins (tauopathy). (Book p574)

questions.q: Deposited inside the neuron, hyperphosphorylated tau forms what, and which sequence follows?
opts: Neurofibrillary tangles -> mitochondrial injury -> progressive neuronal destruction
Amyloid/neuritic plaques -> toxic response from glia
questions.exp: Inside neuron: neurofibrillary tangles -> mitochondrial injury to neurons -> progressive neuronal destruction; outside neuron: amyloid/neuritic plaques elicit toxic response from oligodendrocytes, microglia, astrocytes. (Book p574)

questions.q: In 'type 3 DM / brain diabetes', why does A-beta 42 accumulate?
opts: Hyperinsulinemia uses up the insulin degrading enzyme, leaving A-beta 42 undegraded
questions.exp: Normal physiology: insulin degrading enzyme (IDE) degrades insulin and A-beta 42; in diabetes hyperinsulinemia -> IDE used up in degrading insulin -> A-beta 42 accumulates. (Book p574)

questions.q: The AD pathology list on MRI includes atrophy of which regions?
opts: Median temporal lobe, lateral temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus and entorhinal cortex
questions.exp: Pathology: atrophy of median temporal lobe, lateral temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus and entorhinal cortex (gateway of memory) - seen on MRI; plus Hirano bodies and granulovacuolar degeneration. (Book p574)

questions.q: Depleted cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert justify which DOC class?
questions.exp: Depleted cholinergic neurons of nucleus basalis of meynert -> DOC: cholinesterase inhibitors. (Book p574)

questions.q: The genetic-basis list places Presenilin-1, Presenilin-2 and ApoE4 on which chromosomes respectively?
questions.exp: Genetic basis: Presenilin-1 (chr 14) and Presenilin-2 (chr 1) - m/c defect in familial AD -> early onset -> characteristic features (<45 years, seizures, sleep disturbances); ApoE4 (chr 19) in late-onset dementia, ineffective degradation of A-beta amyloid, most important risk factor (biomarker) for sporadic AD in elderly. (Book p575)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the item that IS a risk factor, against the printed 'Not risk factors' list:
questions.exp: Risk factors: age, positive family history (Presenilin 1 > 2), F > m, h/o head trauma/concussions, h/o stroke, metabolic syndrome, hypertension, diabetes. Printed NOT risk factors: low IQ, smoking, NSAIDs. Note: theory of cognitive reserve - individuals with daily use of cognitive domains are protected from AD. (Book p575)

questions.q: A patient who uses cognitive domains daily is described as protected from AD by which printed theory?
questions.exp: Note - theory of cognitive reserve: individuals with daily use of cognitive domains -> protected from AD. (Book p575)

questions.q: In the clinical-stages loop, naming and comprehension abnormalities (stage II) follow hippocampal stage I and arise at which structure?
opts: Angular gyrus feeding the association areas
questions.exp: Loop: hippocampus -> stage I (Korsakoff amnestic stage: episodic memory loss, difficulty in consolidating memory) -> angular gyrus -> association areas (stage II: stage of anomia, naming and comprehension abnormalities) -> superior parietal lobe praxicons (stage III: visuo-spatial disorientation; apraxia) -> PFC (stage IV: behavioural abnormalities and personality changes). Note: memory = time dependant, contextual, autobiographic. (Book p575)

questions.q: The CSF analysis findings printed for Alzheimer's are:
opts: Down A-beta 42 levels with up hyperphosphorylated tau levels
questions.exp: Investigations: EEG normal/non-specific slowing; CSF analysis down A-beta 42 levels, up hyperphosphorylated tau levels; PET scan IOC detecting hypometabolism and amyloid fibrils (PiB PET scans shown for AD vs control). (Book p576)

questions.q: The PET scan is marked as what for AD, and what does it detect?
questions.exp: PET scan: IOC; detects hypometabolism and amyloid fibrils. (Book p576)

questions.q: The cholinesterase-inhibitor (DOC) list contains which three drugs?
questions.exp: Treatment: 1. cholinesterase inhibitors (DOC): donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine; 2. NMDA antagonist: memantine; 3. monoclonal antibody against A-beta 42: aducanumab. (Book p576)

questions.q: The obsolete drug retired for hepatotoxicity in the note is:
questions.exp: Note: tacrine - obsolete (d/t hepatotoxicity). (Book p576)

units.title: 1. Definition, Domains & Causes
units.guide:
ADL splits and the minor/major cognitive-impairment divide set up the dementia definition.
The six cognitive domains map to their cortical areas; four causes follow with the PFC functions note.

units.title: 2. Reversible Causes & Onset Patterns
units.guide:
The DENTANTIA-style reversible list is read letter by letter with the B12 and NPH notes.
Young-onset and rapidly-progressive lists bracket the pathology note that opens Alzheimer's.

units.title: 3. Alzheimer's Pathogenesis
units.guide:
The APP pathway diverges at A-beta 40/42 into CAA and tauopathy.
Brain diabetes, the MRI atrophy list and the cholinergic DOC follow in printed order.

units.title: 4. Genetics, Risk & Clinical Stages
units.guide:
Presenilin-1/2 and ApoE4 chromosomes set the familial-versus-sporadic split.
Risk factors (and their printed negations) lead into the clinical-stages loop.

units.title: 5. Investigations & Treatment
units.guide:
EEG, CSF and PET lines are read with the MRI and PiB PET image pairs.
The three-line treatment ladder and the tacrine note close Part 1.
